summary: Revisits the advice of RFC 3177 that end sites get /48 blocks of IPv6 space, and obsoletes that recommendation, leaving the exact choice to the operational community. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: How big a chunk of addresses should a home or business get? An old rule said one size. This says it is up to the people running networks.

questions: how big an ipv6 prefix for end sites
what prefix size should an ipv6 end site get
is a /56 enough for a home network
should i assign a /128 to an end site
subtitle: Why the IETF stopped telling everyone to hand out a /48 to every IPv6 end site, and what it asks policy makers to weigh instead.

tldr.problem: RFC 3177 told registries to give every IPv6 end site a /48 by default. That was criticised as wasteful, and the Regional Internet Registries began reconsidering it in 2005.
tldr.mechanism: This document obsoletes the RFC 3177 advice, drops the idea of one default size and the use of /128, and lists the architectural and operational points that any end-site assignment policy should weigh. It leaves the exact size to the operational community.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3177. A /48 is no longer recommended as a single default, but end sites must still get at least one /64 and in most cases significantly more.

today: RFC 6177 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 157) that obsoletes RFC 3177. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RFC 3177 Was Revisited
sections.content:
RFC 3177 called for a default IPv6 assignment of a /48 to each end site. The Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) adopted policies consistent with that, but in 2005 they began discussing the policy again. APNIC, ARIN and RIPE have since revised their end-site policy to encourage smaller blocks, namely /56.

The document focuses on one narrow question: when end sites ask ISPs for IPv6 space, what is an appropriate assignment size? It does not make a formal recommendation on the exact size. That choice is an issue for the operational community, and the IETF's role is limited to guidance on architectural and operational considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who hand out address blocks noticed the old rule gave too much to some and wanted to rethink it. This note gives them advice but lets them decide.

sections.title: What Changes From RFC 3177
sections.content:
The document updates RFC 3177 in three ways.

  • It is no longer recommended that /128s be given out. A site, by definition, implies multiple subnets and multiple devices.
  • RFC 3177 named prefix lengths of /48, /64 and /128. Fixed boundaries risked implementations being hard-coded to them, a return to classful addressing. The intention has always been that there are no hard-coded boundaries and that CIDR applies to all bits of the routing prefixes.
  • A single default size, such as a /48, no longer makes sense for all end sites. End sites come in different shapes and sizes.

One principle is reaffirmed: an end site must be able to obtain a reasonable amount of address space for its actual and planned usage over years. That means at least one /64, and in most cases significantly more.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things changed: no handing out a single address, no fixed set of block sizes baked into software, and no one size for everybody. The promise that everyone gets enough room stays.

sections.title: The Original Reasons for /48
sections.content:
The document looks back at three motivations behind the /48 advice.

First, end sites should easily get enough space without "jumping through hoops". In IPv4 a home user typically gets a single public address, and more usually costs extra. A goal in IPv6 is to change the default from "a single address" to "multiple networks".

Second, a fixed subnet numbering plan simplifies renumbering. A site may use several prefixes at once, including ISP prefixes and Unique Local Addresses, and it is less complex to manage them if the same subnet numbering works for all. Renumbering into a smaller set of subnet bits is often painful. The same simplification applies to managing the reverse ip6.arpa tree in the DNS.

Third, a /48 supports network growth. In IPv4 it is usually hard to get address space for more than a few months of growth, whereas IPv6 lets sites be given space for multi-year growth.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule wanted three things: getting space without a fight, moving house without rearranging every room, and room to grow. Those goals are still good.

sections.title: The Case Against One Size for All
sections.content:
The /48 advice was widely criticised as wasteful. A large business with thousands of employees would by default get the same space as a home user with a small number of devices, and it is hard to argue that home sites will use 65K subnets in the foreseeable future.

Giving homes a single /64 is not the answer either, because it precludes the expectation that even home sites will grow to multiple subnets. So the document still recommends giving home sites significantly more than a single /64, but does not recommend a /48 for every home.

Moving the default for the vast majority of end sites from a /48 to a /56 would save up to 8 bits, reducing the total projected address consumption by up to two orders of magnitude. The exact saving depends on the number of home users relative to larger sites. The goals of RFC 3177 can be met by giving home users a default of less than /48, such as a /56.
sections.plainLanguage: Giving a small family house the same giant plot as a skyscraper wastes land. But a single tiny square is too small, so homes get something in between.

sections.title: Effects on Other Standards
sections.content:
RFC 3177 suggested that some multihoming approaches, such as GSE, might benefit from a fixed /48 boundary. That no longer appears to be a consideration. The argument that one default size spares customers from repeatedly justifying more space still holds as a goal, but it can be reached without giving every end site the same size.

RFC 3056 builds addresses from a public IPv4 address, with a first 48 bits made of a well-known prefix and that address, and a 16-bit subnet field. To ease the move to an ISP-assigned prefix, an end site is advised to number from the rightmost bits first and use the leftmost bits only if its size requires. Similar considerations apply to other documents that allow a 16-bit subnet id, including Unique Local Addresses (RFC 4193).

For IPv6 multicast schemes that embed a unicast prefix (RFC 3306), the assumption is that the prefix is a /64, so the size of the subnet id has no direct impact.
sections.plainLanguage: Other rules that used 16 bits for numbering the rooms still work. Just use the rooms on the right-hand end first.

sections.title: What Policies Should Consider
sections.content:
The summary is plain that a default /48 is not a requirement of the IPv6 architecture: anything of length /64 or shorter works from a standards perspective. But the IETF recommends that any end-site assignment policy take these points into account.

  • It should be easy to obtain space for multiple subnets, meaning more than a single /64, and for reasonable growth over long periods such as a decade or more.
  • The default should reflect the likelihood of needing multiple subnets later, and avoid the IPv4 habit of continual justification for small amounts of extra space.
  • Sites should have enough space to lay out subnets, and not be forced into address conservation such as bridging. Whether bridging is appropriate is an end site matter.
  • Assigning a longer prefix than a site already has is likely to raise its cost and complexity for insufficient benefit.
  • Managing and delegating reverse DNS under ip6.arpa on nibble versus non-nibble boundaries deserves adequate consideration.

The RFC also says a site should never feel compelled to use IPv6-to-IPv6 Network Address Translation because it could not get enough space.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice is a checklist: make it easy to get enough room, plan for growth, do not squeeze people into cramped spaces, and do not shrink what someone already has.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that it has no known security implications. It is a policy guidance document and defines no protocol messages.
sections.plainLanguage: This note is advice for the people handing out addresses, so it does not add any new security worries.
